claims.text: Nanocrystalline grain refinement increases the density of microstructural interfaces.
Increasing microstructural interface density broadens the first-order magnetostructural transition.
Increasing microstructural interface density reduces hysteretic losses during low-field magnetic-cooling cycles.
The as-deposited non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi alloy has an ordered, single-phase hexagonal structure.
The as-deposited FeMnNiGeSi alloy exhibits a sharp, hysteretic first-order magnetostructural transition.
Reducing substrate temperature and/or increasing deposition rate can produce FeMnNiGeSi grain sizes below approximately 100 nm.
Grain sizes below approximately 100 nm increase the density and uniformity of grain boundaries and nanoscale interfaces.
A refined, defect-rich microstructure produces a broad distribution of local magnetic environments or transition behavior.
Grain refinement broadens the distribution of local transformation kinetics.
Distributing the magnetostructural transition spatially produces a smoother magnetic-entropy-change curve and a broader transition.
Nanocrystalline refinement lowers the peak magnetic entropy change relative to the as-deposited baseline.
Nanocrystalline refinement lowers hysteresis during low-field magnetic-cooling cycles.
Nanocrystalline refinement improves effective heat-exchange rates by increasing surface area.
Arc-melted ingots and melt-spun microribbons constitute a coarse-grained baseline with a sharp, high-magnitude, hysteretic entropy change.
The predicted effects hold below an average grain-size threshold of approximately 100 nm and may fail above that threshold.
Prior observations link microstructural defects or integrity to transition kinetics in the proposed alloy.

contradictions.description: The comparison baseline is inconsistent: the initial-state and experiment fields treat conventionally deposited FeMnNiGeSi as the baseline, whereas the dedicated baseline field defines arc-melted ingots and melt-spun microribbons as the baseline.
